when_to_use: Hammond B-3 soul jazz where a communal gospel-blues groove grows from a low simmer into an organ-led testimony, 90-115 BPM

defaults.feel: bluesy swung 8ths, thick backbeat laid behind the grid, organ bass pedal legato

signature_moves: gospel plagal cadence: Bb/F -> F7, heard as reassurance from the room rather than a formal resolution
12-bar gospel-blues turnaround: Gm7 -> C7(#9) -> F7 D7 -> Gm7 C7, keeping testimony and momentum connected
diminished passing chord: Bb7 -> Bbdim7 -> F7, adding one flash of tension before the groove settles back into its body
cadence_options: gospel plagal IV -> I or IV/I -> I when the phrase should feel affirmed by the ensemble
outro hold on 7#9 or 6/9 with an organ smear, allowing the final chord to feel like the room is still vibrating after the players stop
avoid: dense ii-V chains or bebop-level motion; the style gains authority by staying inside sparse gospel-blues language (see soul-jazz-genre.md SS5-6)
a precise big-band ride feel; the backbeat must remain behind the grid and bodily relaxed

hook_archetypes.name: organ-doorway-vamp
hook_archetypes.rhythm: a repeating bass-pedal figure stated alone long enough for the listener to feel invited into the groove before the band answers
hook_archetypes.contour: root-5th pedal under a simple chordal comp, steady and welcoming rather than clever
hook_archetypes.first_appears: Intro, organ alone with slow Leslie so the room is established before the congregation arrives

hook_archetypes.name: testimony-and-amen
hook_archetypes.rhythm: a 2-bar horn statement answered by a 2-bar organ fill, with the reply intensifying the meaning rather than copying the phrase
hook_archetypes.contour: horns deliver a bluesy unison line; organ answers with a gospel-colored chordal rise or fall
hook_archetypes.first_appears: Head, bars 1-4, establishing call-and-response as the social center of the piece

head.note_lengths: clear bluesy phrases that leave room for the organ and band to affirm them
head.contour: singable unison or harmony line over the 12-bar form, with gospel inflection in the targets and turns
head.placement: slightly behind the grid, leaning into the backbeat

organ-solo.note_lengths: phrases lengthen and thicken only as the solo becomes more declarative; begin with speech, not spectacle
organ-solo.contour: start with compact gospel cells, widen the register, then let faster runs emerge near the peak
organ-solo.placement: laid-back at first, pushing forward only when the testimony reaches its strongest point

sax-guitar-solo.note_lengths: shorter blues phrases with space for organ responses; each idea should sound answered by the room
sax-guitar-solo.contour: blues and gospel scale language, shaped by sub-tone warmth or thumb-picked weight rather than technical density

head-return.note_lengths: return to the head clearly, but let one phrase carry the memory of the solos through a changed answer or register
head-return.contour: full band restates the theme with greater communal weight
head-return.placement: behind the grid, now feeling settled rather than tentative

drum_skeleton.low_energy: ride swings gently, thick snare backbeat leans behind 2 and 4, and the closed hat keeps the room grounded under the organ pedal
drum_skeleton.mid_energy: open the hat on selected off-beats and let the kick support the pedal figure, increasing warmth and motion without tightening the feel
drum_skeleton.high_energy: push the ride and thicken snare accents under the solo peak, but preserve the behind-the-grid body of the groove

arrangement_defaults.layout_rules: organ opens alone as host and foundation. Drums enter as a deep communal pulse; guitar adds grain and response; horns finally turn the vamp into a public statement. Let the organ solo grow from murmured phrases to full testimony through registration, density, and interaction. During sax or guitar solos, the organ returns to listening and answering. The head return should feel like everyone now knows the same story. End with a sustained chord and upward organ gesture that leaves the room resonating.

anti_boredom_rules: the organ solo must have a perceptible arc from restraint to declaration; one static registration and phrase density is not enough
keep harmony inside sparse gospel-blues language so changes in touch, response, and intensity remain audible
the backbeat stays behind the grid at every energy level; tightening it changes the social character of the piece
the call-and-response hook must recur with a changed speaker, register, phrase ending, or harmonic answer
comping, fills, horn statements, and solo peaks must remain clearly separated in emphasis so the ensemble sounds responsive rather than crowded

bass_behavior.rhythmic_relationship: locks with kick while sustaining gospel-blues root and fifth motion
bass_behavior.density: continuous but simple, adding passing tones only near peaks
bass_behavior.articulation: legato organ pedal or low drawbar tone

groove_intent.feel: bluesy swung-eighth pocket with a thick laid-back backbeat
groove_intent.kick: supports organ pedal and becomes more present at higher energy
groove_intent.hihat: closed early, sloshier on offbeat accents later
groove_intent.ensemble_relationship: organ pedal and drums create the pocket while horns and organ trade calls and responses

distinguishing_traits: Hammond registration and Leslie speed form the main dynamic arc
organ pedal replaces walking bass and supports a heavy behind-grid backbeat
